transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I just... I didn't really know where else to go. My sister told me I should come in, or maybe it was my supervisor, I don't even remember who brought it up first because everything just kind of blends together lately. I came in because most days I feel like I’m sitting at the bottom of a dark hole. And it's not just a regular sadness, you know? It's like this physical weight on my chest. I'll be at work, fixing a unit or running wires, doing the exact same things I've done for twenty-something years, and I just feel... trapped down there in the dark. 

And it doesn't matter where I am or what I'm doing. Even when I’m around people I know, like the guys on my crew or my own family, I can’t shake this heavy, hopeless feeling. It just clings to me. I try to put on a brave face, I really do, because you can't just stop working and the bills don't pay themselves, but the hole is always there. I'll be sitting in the breakroom with everyone talking and laughing, and I'm just staring at my boots feeling like I'm a million miles away from them and there's no ladder to get back up to the surface. It's just... it's every single day, this heavy darkness. I don't know how else to describe it, but I just can't carry it around anymore.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it's been... gosh, let me think. It's been about a year and two months now. I know the exact timeline because it all started right after this one specific job we were on. We were doing a commercial HVAC install over at that new retail complex, you know, the one they just built off the interstate? I was up there doing some ductwork, just routine stuff, things I’ve done a thousand times since I started in this trade right out of high school. And... I don't know if the footing was loose or if I just lost my balance, but I took a bad fall. 

It left me with a pretty severe back injury. And that was really it. That was the start of it all, because after that fall, it was like... it was like everything just started unraveling. It wasn't just the physical pain, though my back was in absolute agony for weeks, it was being stuck at home, feeling completely useless while my crew was out there working. The medical bills started piling up, the workers' comp paperwork was a nightmare, and I just had way too much time to sit there and think. 

Even when my back finally healed enough for me to get back to work, and I got cleared to go back on the tools, that dark hole I was telling you about had already opened up. It’s like I fell off that scaffolding right into the dark, and I never actually climbed back out. So yeah, a year and two months. Fourteen months of just... dragging myself through every single day, trying to pretend that fall didn't break something else inside me besides just my back. I mean, the physical therapist kept saying I was making great progress, but they don't see how hard it is just to lace up my boots in the morning now, you know? It just feels like everything has been falling apart since that day.
Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before the accident?

No... no, I really don't. And that's... that's honestly one of the hardest parts to wrap my head around, because I used to be such an active person. I mean, my whole life, I was always doing something. I used to love hiking. Every weekend, weather permitting, I'd be out on the trails. I had this whole routine, I'd pack my gear, get out early before the crowds, and just walk for miles. It was my way of clearing my head. And if I wasn't doing that, I was painting. I had this little setup in the corner of my living room, just watercolors mostly, landscapes and things I'd seen on my hikes. It wasn't professional or anything, but it brought me a lot of joy. 

And then there was the makerspace downtown. I used to go there two, maybe three nights a week. I just loved tinkering, you know? Taking things apart, putting them back together, building little gadgets. It was like a puzzle. Honestly, even at work, I used to get a kick out of figuring out a really tricky install. Like when the blueprints didn't quite match the reality of the building, and you had to get creative with the ductwork or the wiring... I used to thrive on that challenge. It felt good to solve it.

But now... now it's just nothing. It's like someone flipped a switch and all the color just drained out of everything. My hiking boots are just sitting in the closet gathering dust. My paints have probably dried out by now because I haven't even looked at them in months. Sometimes I'll stand there in my living room and just stare at my art supplies, or I'll look at the tools I brought home from the makerspace, and I just feel... empty. There's no spark. There's no pull to even pick them up. It just feels like it's not even worth starting. 

And it's affecting my relationships, too. The folks from the makerspace, they used to call and ask where I've been, or if I wanted to come check out a new 3D printer they got, and I just... I ignore the calls. I let them go to voicemail because I don't have the energy to explain that I just don't care anymore. I don't care about the printer, I don't care about the projects, I just don't care. It's too exhausting to even pretend. So I just sit there, looking at my phone ringing, feeling that heavy weight on my chest, knowing I should answer, knowing I used to love talking to them, but I just can't bring myself to do it. It's like all the things that used to make me *me* are just... gone.
Have you ever thought about ending your life since you started feeling this way?

I... gosh, I really don't like talking about this part, but... yes. I have. 

It usually starts in the mornings. I'll just be lying there right before my alarm goes off at 5 AM, staring up at the ceiling, feeling that familiar ache in my lower back before I've even moved a muscle. And I just start thinking that everyone would be so much better off if I just didn’t wake up. If I could just go to sleep and that would be the end of it, you know? Because then I wouldn't have to face another day of being this miserable, heavy burden on everybody. I feel like my sister, the guys on my crew, everyone... they'd just be better off without me dragging down the mood and being so useless. 

But then... well, then it gets darker than just wanting to not wake up. Especially when the mail comes. I've got this massive stack of envelopes on my kitchen island—mostly from the hospital, the physical therapy clinic, the insurance adjusters constantly fighting me on the workers' comp stuff. And when I sit there looking at those numbers, and my back is just screaming at me because I've been on my feet all day running conduit, the pain and the money worries just pile up so high that I feel like I'm suffocating. 

That's when I catch myself. I catch myself actually thinking about ending it. Just... stopping it all myself so I don't have to figure out how to pay another past-due bill or pretend I'm okay on the job site tomorrow. And I'll be completely honest with you, doctor, it scares the living daylights out of me. It really, really scares me. Because I've never been that kind of person. My whole life, I've been the one fixing things. If a commercial unit breaks, I fix it. But I can't fix this. And when my brain goes to that place where I'm actually thinking about how I could just make the pain and the debt stop permanently... it terrifies me. But the thoughts just keep creeping back in anyway, no matter how hard I try to push them away, and I just don't know how to make them stop.
Have you ever experienced any strange or unusual thoughts, such as hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there, since you started feeling this way?

No, no... nothing like that. I mean, I know my mind goes to some pretty dark places, like I was just saying with the... well, you know, wanting it all to stop. But as far as hearing voices or seeing things that aren't actually there? No, definitely not. 

Honestly, sometimes I think it might almost be a distraction if I did, because right now, the only voice I hear in my head is my own, and it just never, ever shuts up. It's just this constant, endless loop of my own voice reminding me of everything that's going wrong. Like, I'll be sitting there in my living room in my recliner—the one I have to sit in because it's the only chair that doesn't make my lower back seize up—and it's so quiet you could hear a pin drop. The TV isn't on, the radio is off, and it's just me and the dead silence. And in that silence, it's just my own thoughts going over and over the insurance forms, or replaying that exact moment on the scaffolding... wondering if I had just placed my left boot an inch to the right, maybe none of this would have happened, maybe I'd still be normal and back with my crew. 

But it's always just me in there. There's no one else talking to me, no voices telling me things, no shadows moving in the corners or anything strange like that. I'm very... I'm very grounded in reality, I guess you could say. It's just that my reality is completely miserable right now. The stack of past-due notices on the kitchen island is real, the throbbing in my spine is real, and the thoughts I have are just my own brain trying to process how much of a total mess my life has become since that fall. So, no, I haven't lost touch with what's real or anything. I don't have any of those strange things happening, just the heavy, exhausting stuff I've been telling you about.
Do you often feel restless, on edge, or have difficulty relaxing?

Restless? I... no, honestly, it's almost the exact opposite of that. I really don't have the energy to be restless anymore. 

It's funny you ask that, because before the accident, sure. If I had to sit still for more than twenty minutes, I'd be bouncing my leg, looking for something to fix, you know? I'd be checking my tools, pacing around the house, looking at the crown molding wondering if I should redo it. I was always on the go. If a weekend rained out my hiking plans and I couldn't get out on the trails, I'd be climbing the walls by noon. I'd end up organizing the garage or taking apart a perfectly good toaster just to put it back together, just doing *something* to burn off that energy. 

But now? Now I just don't have that nervous energy at all. I don't feel on edge or keyed up. I just feel... flat. Heavy, really. Like I was saying about sitting in that recliner in the living room... I just sit there. For hours and hours. It's like my whole body is made of lead. It takes so much effort just to convince myself to get up and get a glass of water from the kitchen, the thought of pacing around or feeling jittery... I just can't even imagine it. 

My sister actually came over last week to check on me, and she was pacing all over my living room, waving her hands around talking about some drama at her office, and honestly, just watching her made me exhausted. I just sat there in my chair, sinking deeper into the cushions, watching her walk back and forth, back and forth, and I remember thinking about how much energy she was wasting. I don't feel like that at all. I just feel like I'm glued to the spot. Even when my thoughts go to those really dark places, like I told you about the bills and the workers' comp stuff, it's not a panicky, restless feeling. It's just this crushing weight. Like I'm at the bottom of the ocean and the water pressure is just pushing me down, holding me completely still. So, no, I wouldn't say I have a hard time relaxing in the sense of being on edge. I'm just... stuck. I'm just completely drained.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight since you started feeling this way?

Weight? Gosh, I don't even own a scale to give you an exact number, but my jeans are definitely fitting weird, because my eating is just completely all over the place right now. It's a total mess. 

I used to be the kind of person who packed a massive lunch cooler every single morning—you have to when you're doing heavy maintenance work and running conduit all day, right? You need the fuel to keep going. But now... now I'll just go pretty much the entire day on nothing but coffee. I'll brew a pot in the morning and just keep refilling my mug while I sit there. The actual thought of making a meal, or even just eating a piece of toast, it literally turns my stomach. Just looking at food in the fridge makes me feel sick, like my throat just completely closes up and rejects the whole idea of chewing and swallowing. So I just drink coffee. Cup after cup, just letting it sit heavy in my gut.

But then... then it'll get to be late at night. Like way late, when the neighborhood is dead quiet and I'm still just planted in that recliner in the living room. And I'll finally realize I haven't had a single solid thing to eat all day and my stomach is cramping up. So I'll force myself up, shuffle into the kitchen—right past that huge stack of insurance papers and medical bills on the island—and I'll just open the pantry cabinet. I don't cook anything. I don't even bother to put anything on a plate or turn on the main overhead light. I just stand there in the dim light and pick at whatever's sitting on the shelf. A handful of dry cereal, some stale crackers, maybe some pretzels I bought three months ago. 

And I'm just chewing it without really tasting it at all. It might as well be sawdust or cardboard for all I care. There's zero enjoyment, zero flavor... I'm just mindlessly putting it in my mouth because my body is hollowed out from running on caffeine for fourteen hours. So, I don't know exactly what the number on the scale says, doctor, but with the way I'm starving all day because food makes me nauseous, and then just grazing on stale junk in the dark without even tasting it... my weight and my appetite are just completely ruined, just like everything else.
Do you find it difficult to initiate or complete tasks due to a lack of energy or motivation?

Energy? Motivation? Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. It's just completely gone. I mean, it's not just about getting up to get a glass of water, like I said before. It's everything. It's the things I used to actually *want* to do. 

Like, I used to be so active, you know? I mentioned the hiking earlier. I used to love getting out on the trails on the weekends, just breathing the fresh air, feeling the burn in my legs. It made me feel alive. And when I wasn't doing that, I was always busy with something else. I loved painting. I had this little corner set up in the spare room with an easel and all my acrylics. I'd lose hours just mixing colors and trying to get a landscape just right. Or I'd head down to the local makerspace. I loved tinkering there, just messing around with the 3D printers or the laser cutter, seeing what I could build. 

Even at work, honestly. I know not everyone loves their job, but when you're an installation and maintenance worker, there's a real satisfaction in figuring out a tricky install. You know, when the blueprints don't quite match the reality of the building, and you have to problem-solve on the fly, routing the conduit in a way that actually works and looks clean? I used to thrive on that. I loved the challenge of it. 

But now... now I just don't care. About any of it. My hiking boots are just sitting by the door, gathering dust. I haven't even looked at them in weeks. The painting stuff... I walked past that spare room the other day and just stared at the blank canvas sitting on the easel, and the tubes of paint, and I just felt... nothing. Just this overwhelming sense of "what's the point?" It just feels like it would take a monumental amount of effort just to squeeze a tube of paint onto a palette, let alone actually create something. 

And the makerspace... the guys there keep calling me, leaving voicemails, asking where I've been, if I want to come down and check out the new CNC router they got. I just watch my phone ring. I don't even have the motivation to pick it up and say "not today." I just let it go to voicemail and ignore it. It's like... none of it feels worth starting. Not a single thing. It's not just that I don't have the physical energy, which I don't, but it's like the part of my brain that used to get excited about things, that used to *want* to do things, is just completely broken. I just sit there and look at all the supplies for my hobbies, or think about the trails, and it's just... dead. It all just feels completely pointless now.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to?

Slowly? Yeah... yeah, I do. It’s actually... it’s exactly how I’ve been trying to explain it to myself. Everything I do is just so incredibly slow now. It’s like... you know when you’re in a swimming pool, right? And you try to walk across the shallow end, and the water is just pushing back against your legs and your arms, making every single movement take twice as much effort and twice as much time? That’s what my entire life feels like right now. I’m just constantly moving like I’m underwater. 

Like I was telling you earlier, about getting up from the couch or that recliner to go into the kitchen for water or to pick at those stale crackers in the dark... it’s not just that I don't have the energy to do it, it’s that when I finally do try, it physically takes me so much longer than it should. I have to sit there and consciously tell my brain, 'okay, move your right foot. Now shift your weight. Now push up.' And even then, my body just kind of slowly drags itself up. The walk down the hallway to the kitchen, which is maybe, what, fifteen feet? It feels like it takes me an eternity just to shuffle over there. 

And it’s not just the physical walking around, either. It’s talking. It’s thinking. Even just answering a really simple question takes me so much longer than it used to. Like when my sister was over, pacing around my living room? She would stop and ask me something completely basic, something like, 'hey, did you remember to check the mail today?' or 'do you want me to order some dinner?' And I would just stare at her. I could hear the words she was saying, but it was like they had to travel through a thick fog just to reach my brain, and then my brain had to slowly piece together what they meant, and then I had to figure out how to make my mouth move to actually answer her. 

She actually stopped talking about her office drama at one point and just looked at me, really concerned, and asked if I was okay, because she said I was responding so slowly and just staring blankly. And it’s not just her, either. If I have to talk to anyone, anywhere, they look at me funny. People keep asking if I’m okay, or if I’m feeling sick, because I just... I move and talk like I’m completely submerged in deep water, and the resistance is just everywhere. I can't just snap out of it or hurry up, no matter how hard I try to force myself to move at a normal speed. It's just all in slow motion.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things that have happened since the accident?

Guilty? God... yeah. Yeah, all the time. It’s honestly all I think about when I’m just sitting there in the quiet. I just... I keep telling myself I’m completely useless now. I mean, look at me. I’ve been working with my hands, doing heavy installation and repair since I was practically out of high school. I always pulled my own weight, I solved the problems on the job site, and now I can't do any of it. I can’t work like I used to, not even close, and it just makes me feel like an absolute waste of space. 

And it’s not just about me, you know? It’s the people I left hanging. I had these apprentices on my crew... young kids, just trying to learn the trade, trying to figure out how to do a commercial install without messing up the whole system. I was supposed to be mentoring them, showing them the ropes, being the one they could rely on. And instead, I just... I vanished on them. I sit in that recliner for hours and I just replay every single apprentice I let down, every time I wasn't there to catch a mistake they made or answer a question. I feel like I just completely abandoned them and set them back. 

And then... then I look at that kitchen island. I told you about the pile of mail, right? The insurance papers? It’s just stacks and stacks of unpaid bills now. Past due notices. Final warnings. And every single envelope just feels like... I don't know, like hard evidence against me. I just stare at them in the dark and replay all of it in my head, like every single unpaid bill just proves that I ruined everything. I ruined my career, I ruined my finances, I let down my crew... I just sit there agonizing over it, running it over and over in my mind, just proving to myself how completely useless I’ve become. It’s like I can’t stop the loop of just blaming myself for every single thing that's fallen apart.
Have you had any periods where you felt somewhat better since the accident, or have your symptoms been constant?

Better? No... no, I haven't had a single day where I felt even a little bit better. It’s just been this... this constant, heavy blanket over everything, every single day. I keep trying to think back, trying to find a day where maybe I woke up and the air didn't feel so thick, or where I didn't feel like I was moving underwater like I told you, but there isn't one. 

It’s been exactly like this, just this endless, crushing weight, for about a year and two months now. I know the exact timeline because I just sit in that chair and replay it over and over. It’s been a year and two months ever since the fall at the HVAC job. 

We were on this commercial site, retrofitting an old warehouse downtown, installing a massive new ventilation system. It was supposed to be a straightforward gig, you know? Just running the ductwork, getting the rooftop units mounted, the kind of work I could do in my sleep. But then I lost my footing. Just one stupid, careless misstep on the scaffolding and I went down hard. That's what left me with the back injury. 

And I thought... I don't know, I thought I'd bounce back. I always bounced back. But ever since that day, ever since I hit the ground and felt my back just give out... everything has just been unraveling. Completely unraveling. First it was the physical pain, and then sitting at home, realizing I couldn't go back to the crew, couldn't help my apprentices, couldn't pay those bills on the counter... and this darkness just settled in. And it hasn't lifted once. Not for a morning, not for an afternoon. It’s just been fourteen solid months of watching my whole life fall apart and not having the energy to stop it.
Have you experienced any periods where you felt detached from reality or had a break from it since the accident?

Detached from reality? Like... like losing my mind, or seeing things that aren't there? No... no, nothing like that. Honestly, doc, I think my problem is the exact opposite. I am way, way too stuck in reality right now. I mean, God, I almost wish I could just detach for a little while, you know? Just float away and get a break from my own head for an afternoon, but... no. I am painfully aware of everything. Every single second of the day, I’m just sitting there in that recliner, and reality is just staring me right in the face, completely crushing me. 

Like, I'll sit there and just watch the dust motes floating in the air when the afternoon sun finally hits the living room window, and I know exactly what time it is, and I know exactly how many hours I've just wasted doing absolutely nothing. I know those past-due notices on the kitchen island are real. I know the pain in my back from the scaffolding is real. I don't have any moments where I forget where I am, or who I am, or what happened. I remember the fall, I remember the exact sound my gear made when it hit the concrete... it’s all just so incredibly real, all the time. 

Sometimes I'll be sitting there in the dark, and like I said earlier, it takes me forever to even move or think, but it's not because I'm not in reality. It's not like my mind is somewhere else. It's just because reality is so heavy, like that deep water I was talking about. It’s just pressing down on me. So no, no breaks from it. No vacations from my own life, as much as I might desperately want one. It's just me, this chair, the silence, and the exact same miserable reality every single day, ticking by so, so slowly...
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or having an inability to sit still?

Fidgeting? Oh, God, no. No, I... I don't have anywhere near the energy to fidget or pace around. It's actually the exact opposite. I sit so still for so long in that recliner that I probably look like a piece of the furniture. 

When I do finally have to move... it's just... everything I do is so incredibly slow now. I mean, just the thought of getting up from the couch and walking into the kitchen to get a glass of water... it feels like I'm planning some massive expedition. It takes me forever just to convince my body to lean forward and stand up. And when I finally do, I'm just dragging myself across the floor. It literally takes me twice, maybe three times as long as it should just to cross the room. 

My sister came by a few days ago to check on me, and she just kept hovering, constantly asking, "Are you okay? Are you sure you're okay?" because I was just... I was trying to make a cup of instant coffee, and it took me what felt like ten minutes just to open the jar and boil the water. She told me I was moving like I was underwater. And that's exactly what it feels like. Like I'm at the bottom of a deep pool, wearing heavy steel-toed work boots, and every single movement is just fighting against this massive, heavy pressure. 

Even just talking... like, answering a simple question from you, or from my sister, it takes me longer than it should. I'll hear the question, and I just sort of stare blankly because my brain takes forever to even find the words, and then my mouth takes forever to actually say them out loud. It's like the connection between my brain and my body is just running on dial-up, you know? Everything is just dragging. So, no... no bouncing my leg or inability to sit still. I'm just stuck in this slow, exhausting crawl all day long.
Are there any activities from your past that you still think about and wish you could participate in?

Activities? I... I don't know. I mean, I try to think about them, but it's like looking at a picture of someone else's life. I used to be so active, doc. I couldn't sit still for a minute before all this happened. 

I used to love hiking. Every weekend, I'd pack up my gear—I had this great lightweight pack, all the right trail shoes, the whole setup—and I'd head up to the state park. I'd spend hours just walking the trails, listening to the birds, feeling the sun. I loved the physical challenge of it, you know? Pushing myself to get to the summit. And painting... I had a whole corner of my spare room set up as a little studio. Watercolors, mostly. I'd paint landscapes from the places I hiked. I loved mixing the colors, trying to get the exact shade of green for the pine trees. 

And then there was the makerspace downtown. I used to go there two, maybe three nights a week. I loved tinkering. I'm an installation worker, right? So I've always been good with my hands, always liked figuring out how things work. I'd build little electronic gadgets, help other people with their projects... I even loved the tricky installs at work. The ones where everyone else on the crew was scratching their heads, looking at the blueprints like they were written in Greek. I'd step in, figure out the angles, get the ductwork to fit perfectly... I loved that feeling of solving a problem.

But now... now I don't wish for any of it. I don't. My hiking boots are just sitting in the closet gathering dust. My watercolor paints are probably all dried up by now. I'll walk past the spare room—well, on the rare occasions I actually get up and walk down the hall—and I'll just stare at the supplies. Just stare at them. And I feel absolutely nothing. No spark, no desire to pick up a brush. 

People from the makerspace have called a few times, leaving voicemails, asking where I've been, if I want to come in and help with this new 3D printer they got... and I just ignore the calls. I watch the phone ring, and I just let it go to voicemail. I don't even want to call them back. It just... none of it feels worth starting. The thought of getting my hiking gear ready, or setting up my paints, or driving down to the makerspace... it just feels pointless. Completely pointless. Why bother? It's just too much effort, and for what? I wouldn't enjoy it anyway. I just... I don't care about any of it anymore. It's all just gone.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual or have difficulty initiating movements?

Yeah, I mean... like I was just saying a minute ago when you asked about the fidgeting, it's exactly that. Everything I do is just so, so slow now. I was just talking about how hard it is to get from the couch to the kitchen, right? It takes me so much longer than it ever should, but it's not even just the walking part. It's the starting part, like you just said. The initiating. I'll just sit there in my chair, and I know I need to stand up, I know I need to go get a glass of water or whatever, and I'll just stare at my feet. My brain is telling my legs to move, but it's like the signal just gets lost somewhere on the way down. 

And then when I finally do manage to force myself up, it's just... I'm dragging. Like I mentioned with my sister, people keep asking if I'm okay because I literally move like I'm underwater. She just hovers and watches me struggle to pour water into a cup, and I can see the worry on her face, but I can't speed up. I just can't. 

And it's not just the physical stuff, either. Even answering a simple question, like I said before, it takes me longer than it should to just find the words and push them out of my mouth. It's like I have to wade through this thick, heavy mud just to do the most basic things. I used to be so quick on my feet, climbing up and down ladders at work all day, hauling heavy tools around without even thinking about it... and now just shifting my weight to stand up feels like this massive, impossible chore. It's just exhausting, doc. Every single movement is just exhausting.
Have you experienced any periods of improvement in your mood or a decrease in depressive symptoms since the accident?

Improvement? No... no, doc. I really wish I could tell you that I've had a good week here or there, or even just a good afternoon, but... no. It’s just been one long, continuous, heavy slog. There hasn't been a single break in the clouds, not even for a minute. 

It’s been exactly like this for about a year and two months now. I know the exact timeframe because it all traces right back to that fall I had at the HVAC job. I was up on a commercial roof, dealing with this incredibly stubborn condenser unit, trying to get some leverage, and I just lost my footing. That fall left me with a bad back injury, and... well, that was the exact moment everything started unraveling. My whole life, just... pulling apart at the seams. 

And for this entire year and two months since it happened, since I had to stop working and climbing and doing everything that made me who I am, it’s just been this same exact heavy, dark, exhausting feeling every single day. I wake up, and it's there waiting for me. I sit in my recliner all day, and it's just pressing down on me. I keep thinking, you know, maybe tomorrow I'll wake up and care about something again, maybe tomorrow the fog will lift just a little bit so I can at least breathe, but it never does. Fourteen months of just... nothing getting better. Not even a tiny bit. It just feels like one endless, terrible day that started a year and two months ago and just refuses to end.
Have you experienced any difficulty in concentrating on things like reading or watching TV since the accident?

TV? Reading? I... I can't even do that anymore. I mean, I'll turn the TV on sometimes just so the house isn't so dead quiet, but I can't follow a single thing that's happening on the screen. I'll sit there for an entire hour and suddenly realize I haven't absorbed a single word of the dialogue, I don't know who the characters are or what they're doing. It's just noise. 

And reading is even worse. It's not just books or magazines, doc, it's everything. I was trying to look at some of my old work stuff recently... you know, just trying to sort through some things I had brought home before the accident. And the paperwork and repair diagrams that used to be completely second nature to me... I mean, I've been doing this for decades, I used to read those HVAC schematics and blueprints like they were children's books. I was the one catching the engineers' mistakes before the crew even started the job. 

But now? Now I look at them and it all just blurs together. The lines, the words, the measurements, it's all just this meaningless, gray blur on the page. It's like my eyes are working fine but the brain behind them is just completely offline. patient.answer:
Activities? I... I don't know. I mean, I try to think about them, but it's like looking at a picture of someone else's life. I used to be so active, doc. I couldn't sit still for a minute before all this happened. 

I used to love hiking. Every weekend, I'd pack up my gear—I had this great lightweight pack, all the right trail shoes, the whole setup—and I'd head up to the state park. I'd spend hours just walking the trails, listening to the birds, feeling the sun. I loved the physical challenge of it, you know? Pushing myself to get to the summit. And painting... I had a whole corner of my spare room set up as a little studio. Watercolors, mostly. I'd paint landscapes from the places I hiked. I loved mixing the colors, trying to get the exact shade of green for the pine trees. 

And then there was the makerspace downtown. I used to go there two, maybe three nights a week. I loved tinkering. I'm an installation worker, right? So I've always been good with my hands, always liked figuring out how things work. I'd build little electronic gadgets, help other people with their projects... I even loved the tricky installs at work. The ones where everyone else on the crew was scratching their heads, looking at the blueprints like they were written in Greek. I'd step in, figure out the angles, get the ductwork to fit perfectly... I loved that feeling of solving a problem.

But now... now I don't wish for any of it. I don't. My hiking boots are just sitting in the closet gathering dust. My watercolor paints are probably all dried up by now. I'll walk past the spare room—well, on the rare occasions I actually get up and walk down the hall—and I'll just stare at the supplies. Just stare at them. And I feel absolutely nothing. No spark, no desire to pick up a brush. 

People from the makerspace have called a few times, leaving voicemails, asking where I've been, if I want to come in and help with this new 3D printer they got... and I just ignore the calls. I watch the phone ring, and I just let it go to voicemail. I don't even want to call them back. It just... none of it feels worth starting. The thought of getting my hiking gear ready, or setting up my paints, or driving down to the makerspace... it just feels pointless. Completely pointless. Why bother? It's just too much effort, and for what? I wouldn't enjoy it anyway. I just... I don't care about any of it anymore. It's all just gone.
